groups.note: If we “get to“ a place, it means we arrive (or reach) there. Before the words “home“, “here“ and “there“, we do not use the word “to“. For example, “I get here at 11 a.m. for my lesson and go home again at 1 p.m.“. The verb “get“ has other meanings besides the ones here, but its general meanings are “become“ (before an adjective) and “obtain“ (before a noun). If you are not sure when to use “get“, it is better to use the other verb with the same meaning. For example, instead of saying “I get many emails“ you can say “I receive many emails“.

groups.note: The difference between “a“ and “an“ is that we use “a“ before a consonant sound whereas we use “an“ before a vowel sound. The difference between “the“ /ðə/ and “the“/ði:/ is the same; we use “the“ /ðə/ before a consonant sound whereas we use “the“/ði:/ before a vowel sound. The noun “use“ starts with the letter “u“, a vowel, but it starts with the sound /j/, a consonant sound. Therefore, we say “the /ðə/ use“ and not “the /ði:/ use“. Remember, some words that begin with the letter “h” start with a vowel sound, because the “h” is silent. For example, we say “an hour“ and not “a hour“.

groups.note: Generally speaking, each verb in English has three forms that you must learn: 1) the present 2) the past 3) the past participle For example, the three forms of the verb “to see“ are “see, saw, seen“, where “see“ is the present, “saw“ is the past, and “seen“ is the past participle. With regular verbs, the 2nd and 3rd forms are the same - for example, “kill, killed, killed“. With irregular verbs, sometimes all the forms are the same – for example, “put, put, put“; sometimes two forms are the same – for example, “come, came, come“; and sometimes all three forms are different – for example, “give, gave, given“.

groups.note: This sentence means that I think there is a real possibility that I will go to the park tomorrow, and, if I do, I will play football. The construction of the 1st conditional is “If“ + present + “will do”. It communicates that we think something is a real possibility.

words: If I went to the park tomorrow, I would play football
groups.note: This sentence means that I think it is very improbable that I will go to the park tomorrow; I am only imagining it. The construction of the 2nd conditional is “If“ + past + “would do”. It communicates that we are only imagining something. It is important to understand that, in the 2nd conditional, we use the past simple after “if“, but we are not thinking about past time; we are thinking about now, the future or general time. examples.q: 1) When do we use “a“ before a word, and when do we use “an“? Give me an example of each.

examples.q: 3) What’s the difference between “any“ and “some“? Give me an example of each.
examples.a: The difference between “any“ and “some“ is that we use “any“ in questions and negative sentences, whereas we use “some“ in positive sentences. examples.q: 4) What’s the difference between the present continuous and the present simple?

examples.q: 5) Where does the preposition generally come in an English sentence with a question word? Give me an example.
examples.a: The preposition generally comes last in an English sentence with a question word. For example, “Who are you speaking to?“

examples.q: 6) What’s the difference between “into“ and “in“? Give me an example of each.
examples.a: The difference between “into“ and “in“ is that we use “into“ for a thing that moves from one place to another, and “in“ for a thing that remains in one place. For example, “I’m putting my hand into my pocket. My hand is in my pocket“.

examples.q: 7) What’s the difference between a possessive adjective and a possessive pronoun? Give me an example of each.
examples.a: The difference between a possessive adjective and a possessive pronoun is that we put a possessive adjective in front of a noun, whereas we use a possessive pronoun instead of a noun. For example, “This is my book. This book is mine“.

examples.q: 8) What are the possessive adjectives?

examples.q: 9) What are the possessive pronouns?

examples.q: 10) When do we use “many“ and “few“ and when do we use “much“ and “little“? Give me an example of each.
examples.a: We use “many“ and “few“ for things we can count, whereas we use “much“ and “little“ for things we can’t count. For example, “many books“, “much water“, “few pens“, “little wine“.

examples.a: We say “cheaper than“, but not “expensiver than“, because the adjective “cheap“ has only one syllable, whereas the adjective “expensive“ has three syllables.

examples.q: 12) Do we use the gerund or the infinitive after a preposition? Give me an example.

examples.q: 13) What is a gerund?

examples.q: 14) What’s the difference between “to look at“ and “to watch“?

examples.q: 15) What’s the difference between “ever“ and “never“?

examples.q: 16) What’s the difference between “quick“ and “quickly“? Give me an example of each.

examples.q: 17) What’s the difference between “over“ and “on“?
examples.a: The difference between “over“ and “on” is that we say “over“ when there is no contact between the two objects, or when one object covers the other completely, whereas we use “on“ when there is contact and when one object doesn’t cover the other completely.

examples.q: 18) How do we form the past tense of regular verbs?
examples.a: We form the past tense of regular verbs by putting the letters “ed“ at the end. For example, “walk – walked“.

examples.q: 19) What’s the difference between “bring“ and “take“?
examples.a: The difference between “bring“ and “take“ is that “bring“ means “carry here“ whereas “take“ means “carry there“. For example, “Bring your book here, please. Take your book home“.

examples.q: 20) When do we use “shall” instead of “will”?
examples.a: We use “shall” instead of “will” when we are making a suggestion with the pronoun “I” or “we“.

examples.q: 21) What are the common ways of asking a question with the verb “to have”?
examples.a: The common ways of asking a question with the verb “to have” are “Do you have a pen?“ and “Have you got a pen?“

examples.q: 22) What do we usually put after the verb “succeed“? Give me an example.
examples.a: We usually put the word “in“ and a gerund after the verb “succeed“. For example, “She always succeeds in getting what she wants“.

examples.q: 23) What’s the difference between “I don’t have to do it“ and “I mustn’t do it“?
examples.a: The difference between “I don’t have to do it“ and “I mustn’t do it“ is that “I don’t have to do it” means that I can do it if I want but it is not necessary, whereas “I mustn’t do it” means that it is bad or wrong to do it.

examples.q: 24) What’s the difference between the present perfect and the past simple? Give me an example of each.
examples.a: The difference between the present perfect and the past simple is that we use the present perfect when we are thinking about time before or up to now, whereas we use the past simple when we are thinking about a specific past time. For example, “I have been here for twenty minutes; I arrived here twenty minutes ago“.

examples.q: 25) Why don’t we usually say “littler“ and “littlest“?
examples.a: We don’t usually say “littler“ and “littlest“ because they’re difficult to pronounce. Instead, we use “smaller“ and “smallest“.

examples.q: 26) What are the three forms of an English verb? Give me an example.
examples.a: The three forms of an English verb are the present, the past and the past participle. For example, “see, saw, seen“.

examples.q: 27) What do we sometimes mean when we use the words “one“, “you“, “we“ and “they“?
examples.a: When we use the words “one”, “you”, “we“ and “they“, we sometimes mean people in general.

examples.q: 28) Which do we generally use the most: “one“, “you“ or “we“?
examples.a: We generally use “you“ the most.

examples.q: 29) What are the three ways in which we can use the present perfect? Give me an example of each.
examples.a: The three ways in which we can use the present perfect are when we talk about our experiences, when we talk about the duration of an action up to now, and when we talk about the result now of a past action.For example, “I’ve read that book; I’ve studied English for two years; I’ve cut my finger“.

examples.q: 30) What’s the difference between “between“ and “among“?
examples.a: The difference between “between“ and “among“ is that we generally use “between“ for two people or things, whereas we use “among“ for more than two people or things.

examples.q: 31) When do we use “to be going to“?
examples.a: We use “to be going to” to say what we think will happen because of something we know now, and to speak about our future intentions. For example, “I think it’s going to rain soon“, and “I’m going to buy a new car“.

examples.q: 32) What are the three forms of the verbs “to be“ and “to go“?
examples.a: The three forms of the verbs “to be“ and “to go“ are “am, was, been“ and “go, went, gone“.

examples.q: 33) Why can I say “Mr Brown has gone to Scotland“, but not “I have gone to Scotland“?
examples.a: Because “I have gone to Scotland“ means I am not here now, which is impossible.

examples.q: 34) What’s the difference between “each other“ and “one another“?
examples.a: The difference between “each other“ and “one another“ is that we generally use “each other“ for two people or things and “one another“ for more than two people or things.

examples.q: 35) What are the past, future and infinitive of “can“?
examples.a: The past of “can“ is “could“ or “was able“; it has no future or infinitive, so we use “will be able“ for the future, and “to be able“ for the infinitive.

examples.q: 36) When do we use the 1st conditional? Give me an example.
examples.a: We use the 1st conditional to communicate that we think something is a real possibility. For example, “If it rains again tomorrow, I will take an umbrella”.

examples.q: 37) When do we use the 2nd conditional? Give me an example.
examples.a: We use the 2nd conditional to communicate that we are only imagining something. For example, “If she had a better job, she would earn more money”.
